title: Phytophotodermatitis & cutaneous amyloid
summary: Plant psoralens plus UVA cause streaky burns then long pigmentation; macular/lichen amyloidosis cause rippled itchy brown patches from chronic friction.

glance.think: Bizarre drip, streak or hand-print burns after gardening or lime cocktails in the sun — later deep brown marks; or rippled itchy interscapular pigment from scratching.
glance.engine: Phototoxic furocoumarin + UVA damage (phyto); keratin-derived amyloid from chronic friction/itch (amyloidosis).
glance.backbone: Wash plant juice off, cool care, short topical steroid, strict sun protection; for amyloid — stop friction, potent steroid ± occlusion, refer if refractory.
glance.never_miss: Child hand-print phytophotodermatitis can mimic non-accidental injury — take a careful plant/sun history.

what: **Phytophotodermatitis** is a non-immune phototoxic reaction when plant **psoralens** on the skin meet **UVA**, causing erythema and blisters in odd shapes, then long-lasting hyperpigmentation. Classic plants: giant hogweed, parsnip, celery, lime, bergamot, fig. **Berloque dermatitis** is perfume bergamot streaks on the neck.
**Macular and lichen amyloidosis** are localised cutaneous amyloidoses: rippled brown macules or itchy keratotic papules from chronic friction, often on the upper back or shins.

list: Psoralens + UVA → epidermal damage and later melanogenesis.
Exposure: strimming, hiking, holiday drinks, cooking with limes.
Amyloid: chronic scratching/friction deposits keratin-derived amyloid in the papillary dermis.
Phyto: burning erythema ± bullae at 24–72 h in streaks/drips/hand-prints; pigmentation weeks later lasting months.
Amyloid: rippled “rippled” brown macular patches (interscapular) or lichenified papules on shins; itch can be severe.
Onset **~24 h (up to 48–72 h)** after contact + sun; peaks 48–72 h.
Burning/stinging (pain > itch), erythema, oedema, vesicles and **bullae** — can resemble partial-thickness burns.
**Bizarre geometric/linear streaks, drips, splash marks, fingerprints/handprints**, on hands, forearms, legs, perioral (citrus), neck (perfume).
Followed by **post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation** that can last months to years — sometimes the presenting complaint (no memory of inflammatory phase).
No systemic features (except large hogweed burns).

diagnosis: Phyto is clinical from shape + exposure history. Amyloid is clinical ± biopsy with special stains when needed.

Clues
rows: Macular amyloid vs LPP / friction PIH

list: Wash plant sap off promptly; cool soaks; leave small blisters intact.
Short topical steroid for inflammation; analgesia; strict sun protection while pigment settles.
Prevention: recognise hogweed, cover arms/legs when strimming, wash after gardening, avoid lime juice on skin in sun.
Stop scrubbing/loofahs; soft clothing; potent topical steroid ± occlusion or topical calcineurin inhibitor for itch.
Emollients; consider sedating antihistamine at night for sleep.
Refer if severe, diagnostic doubt, or for specialist options (retinoids, phototherapy).

management.h: Immediate (after known contact, e.g. hogweed sap)

list: **Wash off sap promptly with soap and water**, cover the skin and keep it **out of sunlight for at least 48 h**; seek advice if eyes affected (rinse, urgent eye assessment).
Cool compresses, emollients, simple analgesia; leave blisters intact or use non-adherent dressings; keep clean (topical antiseptic only if needed).
OTC hydrocortisone 1% for mild small areas (not on broken skin).
**Potent topical corticosteroid** short course (5–7 days) to inflamed intact skin on limbs/trunk; moderate on face. Oral antihistamine if itchy.
Large/extensive blistering, facial/genital/hand burns, signs of infection, or severe pain → **same-day GP/urgent care or burns unit** (giant hogweed burns can need specialist burns care).
Infected blisters: per NICE impetigo/secondary infection guidance.
Reassure — fades slowly over months; **strict sun protection** (tutor: even limited UV re-aggravates); avoid bleaching agents unless specialist-advised.

red_flags: Extensive hogweed burns or eye exposure → urgent assessment.
Safeguarding concern when phytophotodermatitis mimics injury patterns in children.
Systemic amyloid signs are a different disease — this page is localised cutaneous only.
pearls: Pigmentation, not the acute burn, is often why patients attend.
Tell gardeners about giant hogweed — sap plus sun is a classic UK summer presentation.

Other light-related rashes: [polymorphic light eruption](condition:polymorphic-light-eruption), [drug-induced photosensitivity](condition:drug-photosensitivity) and [chronic actinic dermatitis](condition:chronic-actinic-dermatitis).
